grammar_explanation.title: Neuter Gender Category in Marathi
grammar_explanation.explanation: Unlike Hindi which only has Masculine and Feminine genders, Marathi preserves the ancestral Indo-Aryan Neuter gender. Common nouns like 'पाणी' (water), 'पुस्तक' (book), and 'जेवण' (meal) are neuter and take neuter verb/adjective agreements (e.g., 'थोडं पाणी', 'चांगलं पुस्तक').

grammar_explanation.title: Inclusive vs Exclusive 'We' ('आम्ही' vs 'आपण')
grammar_explanation.explanation: Marathi strictly distinguishes 'आम्ही' (we excluding the listener) from 'आपण' (we including the listener). Hindi uses 'हम' for both, often leading to communicative ambiguity.

grammar_explanation.title: Yes/No Question Marker ('क्या ... ?' vs '... का?')
grammar_explanation.explanation: In Hindi, yes/no questions start with 'क्या' ('क्या सब ठीक है?'). In Marathi, speakers place the question particle 'का' (ka) at the end of the sentence ('सगळं ठीक आहे का?').

differences: Three-Gender System: Marathi features a 3rd grammatical gender (नपुंसकलिंग / Neuter). Modifiers take neuter endings ('माझं नाव', 'थोडं पाणी').
Clusivity Distinction: Marathi has two words for 'we': 'आपण' (includes the listener) and 'आम्ही' (excludes the listener).
Question Word Order: Hindi begins yes/no questions with 'क्या', while Marathi appends 'का' (ka) to the end.
Register & Tone: Formal / Respectful (Used when addressing elders, professors, clients, strangers, or in professional workplaces.)
common_mistakes: Avoid literal word-by-word substitution; Marathi postpositions attach directly to nouns rather than standing as separate words.

examples.english_translation: I want cold water (water is neuter).
This is my book (book is neuter: 'हे' / 'माझं').
What is your name? ('नाव' is neuter: 'तुझं').

grammar_explanation.explanation: Unlike Hindi which only has Masculine and Feminine genders, Marathi preserves the ancestral Indo-Aryan Neuter gender. Common nouns like 'पाणी' (water), 'पुस्तक' (book), and 'जेवण' (meal) are neuter and take neuter verb/adjective agreements (e.g., 'थोडं पाणी', 'चांगलं पुस्तक').

grammar_explanation.title: Inclusive vs Exclusive 'We' ('आम्ही' vs 'आपण')
grammar_explanation.explanation: Marathi strictly distinguishes 'आम्ही' (we excluding the listener) from 'आपण' (we including the listener). Hindi uses 'हम' for both, often leading to communicative ambiguity.

grammar_explanation.title: Yes/No Question Marker ('क्या ... ?' vs '... का?')
grammar_explanation.explanation: In Hindi, yes/no questions start with 'क्या' ('क्या सब ठीक है?'). In Marathi, speakers place the question particle 'का' (ka) at the end of the sentence ('सगळं ठीक आहे का?').

differences: Three-Gender System: Marathi features a 3rd grammatical gender (नपुंसकलिंग / Neuter). Modifiers take neuter endings ('माझं नाव', 'थोडं पाणी').
Clusivity Distinction: Marathi has two words for 'we': 'आपण' (includes the listener) and 'आम्ही' (excludes the listener).
Question Word Order: Hindi begins yes/no questions with 'क्या', while Marathi appends 'का' (ka) to the end.
Register & Tone: Formal / Respectful (Used when addressing elders, professors, clients, strangers, or in professional workplaces.)
common_mistakes: Avoid literal word-by-word substitution; Marathi postpositions attach directly to nouns rather than standing as separate words.

grammar_explanation.title: Gender Agreement with Languages
grammar_explanation.explanation: In both Hindi and Marathi, names of languages are grammatically feminine. Hence, 'सीखना' becomes 'सीखनी' in Hindi and 'शिकायचे' becomes feminine 'शिकायची' in Marathi.

grammar_explanation.title: Cognate Root with Sound Shift (s -> sh)
grammar_explanation.explanation: The verb root corresponds systematically: Hindi 'सीख' (seekh) corresponds to Marathi 'शिक' (shik).

differences: Gender Concord: Both languages treat language names as feminine; verbs inflect to feminine ('सीखनी है' / 'शिकायची आहे').
Phonetic Shift: Regular sibilant correspondence where Hindi /s/ aligns with Marathi /sh/ ('सीख' -> 'शिक').
Dative Subject: Intent to learn uses dative experiencer ('मुझे' -> 'मला').
common_mistakes: Using masculine verb form 'शिकायचा आहे' instead of feminine 'शिकायची आहे' when referring to Marathi.
Saying nominative 'मी मराठी शिकायची आहे' instead of dative 'मला मराठी शिकायची आहे'.

grammar_explanation.explanation: In both Hindi and Marathi, names of spoken languages (मराठी, हिंदी, इंग्रजी) are grammatically feminine. Verbs agreeing with language names reflect feminine inflection ('सीखनी है' / 'शिकायची आहे').

grammar_explanation.title: Temporal Distinction ('कल' vs 'उद्या')
grammar_explanation.explanation: Hindi 'कल' is ambiguous and denotes either yesterday or tomorrow depending solely on verb tense. Marathi strictly requires 'उद्या' (udya) for tomorrow and 'काल' (kaal) for yesterday.

grammar_explanation.title: Inclusive vs Exclusive 'We' ('आम्ही' vs 'आपण')
grammar_explanation.explanation: Marathi strictly distinguishes 'आम्ही' (we excluding the listener) from 'आपण' (we including the listener). Hindi uses 'हम' for both, often leading to communicative ambiguity.

grammar_explanation.title: Yes/No Question Marker ('क्या ... ?' vs '... का?')
grammar_explanation.explanation: In Hindi, yes/no questions start with 'क्या' ('क्या सब ठीक है?'). In Marathi, speakers place the question particle 'का' (ka) at the end of the sentence ('सगळं ठीक आहे का?').

differences: Temporal Clarity: Hindi 'कल' relies entirely on tense context; Marathi never confuses them: 'उद्या' (future) vs 'काल' (past).
Clusivity Distinction: Marathi has two words for 'we': 'आपण' (includes the listener) and 'आम्ही' (excludes the listener).
Question Word Order: Hindi begins yes/no questions with 'क्या', while Marathi appends 'का' (ka) to the end.
Synthetic Suffixation: In 'कल' → 'उद्या', Marathi attaches grammatical markers directly as word suffixes, unlike Hindi analytic postpositions.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'काल' (yesterday) with 'उद्या' (tomorrow). In Hindi, 'कल' means both yesterday and tomorrow, but in Marathi 'काल' strictly means yesterday. 💡 Tip: Always use 'उद्या' (udya) when referring to future actions.

grammar_explanation.title: Direct Locative Suffix ('-त' / '-ी')
grammar_explanation.source_pattern: पुणे में / घर पर / नाश्ते में
grammar_explanation.explanation: Marathi frequently uses synthetic case suffixes '-त' (in) and '-ी' (at/home) directly attached to an inflected oblique noun root (e.g. 'पुण्यात' = in Pune, 'घरी' = at home), whereas Hindi uses independent postpositions ('में', 'पर').

grammar_explanation.title: Inclusive vs Exclusive 'We' ('आम्ही' vs 'आपण')
grammar_explanation.explanation: Marathi strictly distinguishes 'आम्ही' (we excluding the listener) from 'आपण' (we including the listener). Hindi uses 'हम' for both, often leading to communicative ambiguity.

grammar_explanation.title: Present Continuous Aspect ('-रहा हूँ' vs '-त आहे')
grammar_explanation.source_pattern: जा रहा हूँ / आ रहा हूँ (-raha hoon)
grammar_explanation.explanation: Hindi forms continuous aspect using the separate auxiliary participle 'रहा हूँ / रहे हैं' ('मैं जा रहा हूँ' = I am going). Marathi directly suffixes imperfective '-त' (-t) to the verb root plus 'आहे' ('मी जात आहे'). Notice Marathi has no separate word for 'रहा'; the '-त' suffix fulfills that role.

differences: Locative Suffixation: Hindi uses analytic postpositions ('घर पर', 'पुणे में'), while Marathi fuses suffixes directly into nouns ('घरी', 'पुण्यात').
Clusivity Distinction: Marathi has two words for 'we': 'आपण' (includes the listener) and 'आम्ही' (excludes the listener).
Aspect Suffix vs Particle: Marathi has no separate word for Hindi 'रहा'; instead, it attaches the suffix '-त' directly to the verb stem ('जात आहे').
Register & Tone: Neutral / Standard (Standard communicative tone appropriate in everyday contexts.)
common_mistakes: Avoid literal word-by-word substitution; Marathi postpositions attach directly to nouns rather than standing as separate words.

grammar_explanation.title: Direct Locative Suffix ('-त' / '-ी')
grammar_explanation.target_pattern: पुणे में / घर पर / नाश्ते में
grammar_explanation.explanation: Marathi frequently uses synthetic case suffixes '-त' (in) and '-ी' (at/home) directly attached to an inflected oblique noun root (e.g. 'पुण्यात' = in Pune, 'घरी' = at home), whereas Hindi uses independent postpositions ('में', 'पर').

grammar_explanation.title: Inclusive vs Exclusive 'We' ('आम्ही' vs 'आपण')
grammar_explanation.explanation: Marathi strictly distinguishes 'आम्ही' (we excluding the listener) from 'आपण' (we including the listener). Hindi uses 'हम' for both, often leading to communicative ambiguity.

differences: Locative Suffixation: Hindi uses analytic postpositions ('घर पर', 'पुणे में'), while Marathi fuses suffixes directly into nouns ('घरी', 'पुण्यात').
Clusivity Distinction: Marathi has two words for 'we': 'आपण' (includes the listener) and 'आम्ही' (excludes the listener).
Synthetic Suffixation: In 'घरी' → 'घर', Marathi attaches grammatical markers directly as word suffixes, unlike Hindi analytic postpositions.
Register & Tone: Neutral / Standard (Standard communicative tone appropriate in everyday contexts.)
common_mistakes: Avoid literal word-by-word substitution; Marathi postpositions attach directly to nouns rather than standing as separate words.

grammar_explanation.title: Temporal Distinction ('कल' vs 'उद्या')
grammar_explanation.explanation: Hindi 'कल' is ambiguous and denotes either yesterday or tomorrow depending solely on verb tense. Marathi strictly requires 'उद्या' (udya) for tomorrow and 'काल' (kaal) for yesterday.

differences: Temporal Clarity: Hindi 'कल' relies entirely on tense context; Marathi never confuses them: 'उद्या' (future) vs 'काल' (past).
Register & Tone: Neutral / Standard (Standard communicative tone appropriate in everyday contexts.)
common_mistakes: Confusing 'काल' (yesterday) with 'उद्या' (tomorrow). In Hindi, 'कल' means both yesterday and tomorrow, but in Marathi 'काल' strictly means yesterday. 💡 Tip: Always use 'उद्या' (udya) when referring to future actions.

examples.english_translation: I will go to college tomorrow.

grammar_explanation.source_pattern: जा रहा हूँ / आ रहा हूँ (-raha hoon)
grammar_explanation.explanation: Hindi forms continuous aspect using the separate auxiliary participle 'रहा हूँ / रहे हैं' ('मैं जा रहा हूँ' = I am going). Marathi directly suffixes imperfective '-त' (-t) to the verb root plus 'आहे' ('मी जात आहे'). Notice Marathi has no separate word for 'रहा'; the '-त' suffix fulfills that role.

differences: Aspect Suffix vs Particle: Marathi has no separate word for Hindi 'रहा'; instead, it attaches the suffix '-त' directly to the verb stem ('जात आहे').
Synthetic Suffixation: In 'मुझे' → 'मला', Marathi attaches grammatical markers directly as word suffixes, unlike Hindi analytic postpositions.
Register & Tone: Neutral / Standard (Standard communicative tone appropriate in everyday contexts.)
common_mistakes: Attempting to literally translate Hindi 'रहा' into Marathi (e.g., saying 'मी राहतो आहे' instead of 'मी जात आहे'). 💡 Tip: In Marathi, simply add suffix '-त' (-t) to the verb root plus 'आहे': 'जा' + 'त' = 'जात आहे' (jaat aahe).

grammar_explanation.title: Temporal Distinction ('कल' vs 'उद्या')
grammar_explanation.explanation: Hindi 'कल' is ambiguous and denotes either yesterday or tomorrow depending solely on verb tense. Marathi strictly requires 'उद्या' (udya) for tomorrow and 'काल' (kaal) for yesterday.

grammar_explanation.title: Inclusive vs Exclusive 'We' ('आम्ही' vs 'आपण')
grammar_explanation.explanation: Marathi strictly distinguishes 'आम्ही' (we excluding the listener) from 'आपण' (we including the listener). Hindi uses 'हम' for both, often leading to communicative ambiguity.

grammar_explanation.title: Yes/No Question Marker ('क्या ... ?' vs '... का?')
grammar_explanation.explanation: In Hindi, yes/no questions start with 'क्या' ('क्या सब ठीक है?'). In Marathi, speakers place the question particle 'का' (ka) at the end of the sentence ('सगळं ठीक आहे का?').

differences: Temporal Clarity: Hindi 'कल' relies entirely on tense context; Marathi never confuses them: 'उद्या' (future) vs 'काल' (past).
Clusivity Distinction: Marathi has two words for 'we': 'आपण' (includes the listener) and 'आम्ही' (excludes the listener).
Question Word Order: Hindi begins yes/no questions with 'क्या', while Marathi appends 'का' (ka) to the end.
Register & Tone: Neutral / Standard (Standard communicative tone appropriate in everyday contexts.)
common_mistakes: Confusing 'काल' (yesterday) with 'उद्या' (tomorrow). In Hindi, 'कल' means both yesterday and tomorrow, but in Marathi 'काल' strictly means yesterday. 💡 Tip: Always use 'उद्या' (udya) when referring to future actions.

grammar_explanation.title: Temporal Distinction ('कल' vs 'उद्या')
grammar_explanation.explanation: Hindi 'कल' is ambiguous and denotes either yesterday or tomorrow depending solely on verb tense. Marathi strictly requires 'उद्या' (udya) for tomorrow and 'काल' (kaal) for yesterday.

grammar_explanation.title: Neuter Gender Category in Marathi
grammar_explanation.explanation: Unlike Hindi which only has Masculine and Feminine genders, Marathi preserves the ancestral Indo-Aryan Neuter gender. Common nouns like 'पाणी' (water), 'पुस्तक' (book), and 'जेवण' (meal) are neuter and take neuter verb/adjective agreements (e.g., 'थोडं पाणी', 'चांगलं पुस्तक').

grammar_explanation.title: Yes/No Question Marker ('क्या ... ?' vs '... का?')
grammar_explanation.explanation: In Hindi, yes/no questions start with 'क्या' ('क्या सब ठीक है?'). In Marathi, speakers place the question particle 'का' (ka) at the end of the sentence ('सगळं ठीक आहे का?').

differences: Temporal Clarity: Hindi 'कल' relies entirely on tense context; Marathi never confuses them: 'उद्या' (future) vs 'काल' (past).
Three-Gender System: Marathi features a 3rd grammatical gender (नपुंसकलिंग / Neuter). Modifiers take neuter endings ('माझं नाव', 'थोडं पाणी').
Question Word Order: Hindi begins yes/no questions with 'क्या', while Marathi appends 'का' (ka) to the end.
Register & Tone: Neutral / Standard (Standard communicative tone appropriate in everyday contexts.)
common_mistakes: Confusing 'काल' (yesterday) with 'उद्या' (tomorrow). In Hindi, 'कल' means both yesterday and tomorrow, but in Marathi 'काल' strictly means yesterday. 💡 Tip: Always use 'उद्या' (udya) when referring to future actions.

grammar_explanation.title: Temporal Distinction ('कल' vs 'उद्या')
grammar_explanation.explanation: Hindi 'कल' is ambiguous and denotes either yesterday or tomorrow depending solely on verb tense. Marathi strictly requires 'उद्या' (udya) for tomorrow and 'काल' (kaal) for yesterday.

differences: Temporal Clarity: Hindi 'कल' relies entirely on tense context; Marathi never confuses them: 'उद्या' (future) vs 'काल' (past).
Synthetic Suffixation: In 'कल' → 'उद्या', Marathi attaches grammatical markers directly as word suffixes, unlike Hindi analytic postpositions.
Register & Tone: Neutral / Standard (Standard communicative tone appropriate in everyday contexts.)
common_mistakes: Confusing 'काल' (yesterday) with 'उद्या' (tomorrow). In Hindi, 'कल' means both yesterday and tomorrow, but in Marathi 'काल' strictly means yesterday. 💡 Tip: Always use 'उद्या' (udya) when referring to future actions.

examples.english_translation: I will go to college tomorrow.

grammar_explanation.title: Temporal Distinction ('कल' vs 'उद्या')
grammar_explanation.explanation: Hindi 'कल' is ambiguous and denotes either yesterday or tomorrow depending solely on verb tense. Marathi strictly requires 'उद्या' (udya) for tomorrow and 'काल' (kaal) for yesterday.

differences: Temporal Clarity: Hindi 'कल' relies entirely on tense context; Marathi never confuses them: 'उद्या' (future) vs 'काल' (past).
Synthetic Suffixation: In 'मुझे' → 'मला', Marathi attaches grammatical markers directly as word suffixes, unlike Hindi analytic postpositions.
Register & Tone: Neutral / Standard (Standard communicative tone appropriate in everyday contexts.)
common_mistakes: Confusing 'काल' (yesterday) with 'उद्या' (tomorrow). In Hindi, 'कल' means both yesterday and tomorrow, but in Marathi 'काल' strictly means yesterday. 💡 Tip: Always use 'उद्या' (udya) when referring to future actions.

examples.english_translation: I will go to college tomorrow.

grammar_explanation.title: Neuter Gender Category in Marathi
grammar_explanation.explanation: Unlike Hindi which only has Masculine and Feminine genders, Marathi preserves the ancestral Indo-Aryan Neuter gender. Common nouns like 'पाणी' (water), 'पुस्तक' (book), and 'जेवण' (meal) are neuter and take neuter verb/adjective agreements (e.g., 'थोडं पाणी', 'चांगलं पुस्तक').

differences: Three-Gender System: Marathi features a 3rd grammatical gender (नपुंसकलिंग / Neuter). Modifiers take neuter endings ('माझं नाव', 'थोडं पाणी').
Register & Tone: Neutral / Standard (Standard communicative tone appropriate in everyday contexts.)
common_mistakes: Avoid literal word-by-word substitution; Marathi postpositions attach directly to nouns rather than standing as separate words.

grammar_explanation.title: Dative Destination Suffix ('-ला')
grammar_explanation.explanation: Marathi attaches the dative postposition '-ला' (-la) directly to destination nouns (e.g. 'कॉलेजला', 'ऑफिसला') to indicate direction or recipient. Colloquial Hindi often leaves destinations unmarked.

grammar_explanation.title: Direct Locative Suffix ('-त' / '-ी')
grammar_explanation.source_pattern: पुणे में / घर पर / नाश्ते में
grammar_explanation.explanation: Marathi frequently uses synthetic case suffixes '-त' (in) and '-ी' (at/home) directly attached to an inflected oblique noun root (e.g. 'पुण्यात' = in Pune, 'घरी' = at home), whereas Hindi uses independent postpositions ('में', 'पर').

grammar_explanation.title: Yes/No Question Marker ('क्या ... ?' vs '... का?')
grammar_explanation.explanation: In Hindi, yes/no questions start with 'क्या' ('क्या सब ठीक है?'). In Marathi, speakers place the question particle 'का' (ka) at the end of the sentence ('सगळं ठीक आहे का?').

differences: Synthetic Destination Marker: Marathi explicitly suffixes '-ला' to destination nouns ('कॉलेज' -> 'कॉलेजला'), while Hindi leaves it bare.
Locative Suffixation: Hindi uses analytic postpositions ('घर पर', 'पुणे में'), while Marathi fuses suffixes directly into nouns ('घरी', 'पुण्यात').
Question Word Order: Hindi begins yes/no questions with 'क्या', while Marathi appends 'का' (ka) to the end.
Register & Tone: Neutral / Standard (Standard communicative tone appropriate in everyday contexts.)
common_mistakes: Omitting the dative destination suffix '-ला' in Marathi (e.g., saying 'कॉलेज जायचं' instead of 'कॉलेजला जायचं'). 💡 Tip: Marathi attaches '-ला' directly to the destination noun when indicating travel toward it.

Attempting to literally translate Hindi 'रहा' into Marathi (e.g., saying 'मी राहतो आहे' instead of 'मी जात आहे'). 💡 Tip: In Marathi, simply add suffix '-त' (-t) to the verb root plus 'आहे': 'जा' + 'त' = 'जात आहे' (jaat aahe).

grammar_explanation.explanation: Marathi frequently uses synthetic case suffixes '-त' (in) and '-ी' (at/home) directly attached to an inflected oblique noun root (e.g. 'पुण्यात' = in Pune, 'घरी' = at home), whereas Hindi uses independent postpositions ('में', 'पर').

grammar_explanation.title: Yes/No Question Marker ('क्या ... ?' vs '... का?')
grammar_explanation.explanation: In Hindi, yes/no questions start with 'क्या' ('क्या सब ठीक है?'). In Marathi, speakers place the question particle 'का' (ka) at the end of the sentence ('सगळं ठीक आहे का?').

differences: Synthetic Destination Marker: Marathi explicitly suffixes '-ला' to destination nouns ('कॉलेज' -> 'कॉलेजला'), while Hindi leaves it bare.
Locative Suffixation: Hindi uses analytic postpositions ('घर पर', 'पुणे में'), while Marathi fuses suffixes directly into nouns ('घरी', 'पुण्यात').
Question Word Order: Hindi begins yes/no questions with 'क्या', while Marathi appends 'का' (ka) to the end.
Register & Tone: Neutral / Standard (Standard communicative tone appropriate in everyday contexts.)
common_mistakes: Omitting the dative destination suffix '-ला' in Marathi (e.g., saying 'कॉलेज जायचं' instead of 'कॉलेजला जायचं'). 💡 Tip: Marathi attaches '-ला' directly to the destination noun when indicating travel toward it.

Attempting to literally translate Hindi 'रहा' into Marathi (e.g., saying 'मी राहतो आहे' instead of 'मी जात आहे'). 💡 Tip: In Marathi, simply add suffix '-त' (-t) to the verb root plus 'आहे': 'जा' + 'त' = 'जात आहे' (jaat aahe).

examples.english_translation: I have to go to the office.
He is going to the station.
We are going to the market.

grammar_explanation.explanation: Both Hindi and Marathi share core Subject-Object-Verb (SOV) sentence order and postpositional phrasing.

differences: Register & Tone: Neutral / Standard (Standard communicative tone appropriate in everyday contexts.)
Word Order: Both languages follow Subject-Object-Verb (SOV) order, but Marathi maintains strict gender-number agreement with neuter nouns.
common_mistakes: Avoid literal word-by-word substitution; Marathi postpositions attach directly to nouns rather than standing as separate words.

grammar_explanation.title: Direct Locative Suffix ('-त' / '-ी')
grammar_explanation.source_pattern: पुणे में / घर पर / नाश्ते में
grammar_explanation.explanation: Marathi frequently uses synthetic case suffixes '-त' (in) and '-ी' (at/home) directly attached to an inflected oblique noun root (e.g. 'पुण्यात' = in Pune, 'घरी' = at home), whereas Hindi uses independent postpositions ('में', 'पर').

differences: Locative Suffixation: Hindi uses analytic postpositions ('घर पर', 'पुणे में'), while Marathi fuses suffixes directly into nouns ('घरी', 'पुण्यात').
Register & Tone: Neutral / Standard (Standard communicative tone appropriate in everyday contexts.)
common_mistakes: Avoid literal word-by-word substitution; Marathi postpositions attach directly to nouns rather than standing as separate words.

grammar_explanation.source_pattern: जा रहा हूँ / आ रहा हूँ (-raha hoon)
grammar_explanation.explanation: Hindi forms continuous aspect using the separate auxiliary participle 'रहा हूँ / रहे हैं' ('मैं जा रहा हूँ' = I am going). Marathi directly suffixes imperfective '-त' (-t) to the verb root plus 'आहे' ('मी जात आहे'). Notice Marathi has no separate word for 'रहा'; the '-त' suffix fulfills that role.

differences: Aspect Suffix vs Particle: Marathi has no separate word for Hindi 'रहा'; instead, it attaches the suffix '-त' directly to the verb stem ('जात आहे').

common_mistakes: Avoid literal word-by-word substitution; Marathi postpositions attach directly to nouns rather than standing as separate words.

grammar_explanation.title: Neuter Gender Category in Marathi
grammar_explanation.explanation: Unlike Hindi which only has Masculine and Feminine genders, Marathi preserves the ancestral Indo-Aryan Neuter gender. Common nouns like 'पाणी' (water), 'पुस्तक' (book), and 'जेवण' (meal) are neuter and take neuter verb/adjective agreements (e.g., 'थोडं पाणी', 'चांगलं पुस्तक').

grammar_explanation.explanation: Unlike Hindi which only has Masculine and Feminine genders, Marathi preserves the ancestral Indo-Aryan Neuter gender. Common nouns like 'पाणी' (water), 'पुस्तक' (book), and 'जेवण' (meal) are neuter and take neuter verb/adjective agreements (e.g., 'थोडं पाणी', 'चांगलं पुस्तक').

differences: Three-Gender System: Marathi features a 3rd grammatical gender (नपुंसकलिंग / Neuter). Modifiers take neuter endings ('माझं नाव', 'थोडं पाणी').
Register & Tone: Neutral / Standard (Standard communicative tone appropriate in everyday contexts.)
common_mistakes: Avoid literal word-by-word substitution; Marathi postpositions attach directly to nouns rather than standing as separate words.

grammar_explanation.title: Temporal Distinction ('कल' vs 'उद्या')
grammar_explanation.explanation: Hindi 'कल' is ambiguous and denotes either yesterday or tomorrow depending solely on verb tense. Marathi strictly requires 'उद्या' (udya) for tomorrow and 'काल' (kaal) for yesterday.

differences: Temporal Clarity: Hindi 'कल' relies entirely on tense context; Marathi never confuses them: 'उद्या' (future) vs 'काल' (past).
Synthetic Suffixation: In 'कल' → 'उद्या', Marathi attaches grammatical markers directly as word suffixes, unlike Hindi analytic postpositions.
Register & Tone: Neutral / Standard (Standard communicative tone appropriate in everyday contexts.)
common_mistakes: Confusing 'काल' (yesterday) with 'उद्या' (tomorrow). In Hindi, 'कल' means both yesterday and tomorrow, but in Marathi 'काल' strictly means yesterday. 💡 Tip: Always use 'उद्या' (udya) when referring to future actions.

examples.english_translation: I will go to college tomorrow.

grammar_explanation.title: Temporal Distinction ('कल' vs 'उद्या')
grammar_explanation.explanation: Hindi 'कल' is ambiguous and denotes either yesterday or tomorrow depending solely on verb tense. Marathi strictly requires 'उद्या' (udya) for tomorrow and 'काल' (kaal) for yesterday.

differences: Temporal Clarity: Hindi 'कल' relies entirely on tense context; Marathi never confuses them: 'उद्या' (future) vs 'काल' (past).
Synthetic Suffixation: In 'उद्या' → 'कल', Marathi attaches grammatical markers directly as word suffixes, unlike Hindi analytic postpositions.
Register & Tone: Neutral / Standard (Standard communicative tone appropriate in everyday contexts.)
common_mistakes: Confusing 'काल' (yesterday) with 'उद्या' (tomorrow). In Hindi, 'कल' means both yesterday and tomorrow, but in Marathi 'काल' strictly means yesterday. 💡 Tip: Always use 'उद्या' (udya) when referring to future actions.
